questions.sec: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: PPH is the most common cause of maternal mortality in India. Match the blood-loss definition – after vaginal delivery : after C-section : ACOG (any delivery).
questions.exp: PPH ≥500 mL after vaginal delivery, ≥1000 mL after C-section; ACOG ≥1000 mL after any delivery. (Book p528)

questions.sec: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three clinical definitions of PPH?
opts: Fall in haemoglobin by ≥2 g/dL
Excessive bleeding after delivery requiring blood transfusion
Blood loss with signs and symptoms of hypovolemia
Fall in hematocrit by ≥10% between admission and postpartum period
questions.exp: Clinical definitions: need for transfusion, hypovolemic signs, ≥10% hematocrit fall. Severe PPH (WHO) = ≥1000 mL. (Book p528)

questions.sec: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: Fill up: Primary PPH occurs within ______ of delivery, and secondary PPH runs from 24 hours to ______ afterwards.
opts: 24 hours; 12 weeks
6 hours; 24 hours
1 hour; 7 days
48 hours; 6 weeks
questions.exp: Primary PPH is within 24 hours of birth and secondary PPH runs from 24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum. (Book p528)

questions.sec: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: Match the 4 Ts with the m/c examples – Tone : Trauma : Thrombin : Tissue.
opts: Atonic uterus : perineal tear or rupture : bleeding disorders : retained placental tissue
Retained placental tissue : atonic uterus : perineal tear or rupture : bleeding disorders
Bleeding disorders : retained placental tissue : atonic uterus : perineal tear or rupture
Perineal tear or rupture : bleeding disorders : atonic uterus : retained placental tissue
questions.exp: The 4 Ts: Tone – atonic uterus (commonest overall and commonest primary PPH); Trauma – perineal or cervical tear, hematoma, rupture; Thrombin – bleeding disorders; Tissue – retained placental tissue (commonest secondary PPH). (Book p528)

questions.sec: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: The 'living ligature' of the uterus refers to:
opts: The interlacing middle layer of myometrium, whose fibres compress the vessels as the uterus contracts
The round ligament, which anchors the uterus and kinks the ovarian vessels after delivery
The internal cervical os, which closes and compresses the cervical branch of the uterine artery
The decidua basalis, whose spiral arteries thrombose spontaneously after separation of the placenta
questions.exp: The middle myometrial fibres act as living ligatures; when they fail to contract and retract, the sinuses bleed and atonic PPH follows. (Book p528)

questions.sec: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: A woman undergoes postpartum dilatation and curettage for retained products of conception. What is she at the highest risk of, and what best prevents PPH in the first place?
opts: Asherman syndrome; active management of the third stage of labour
Uterine inversion; an oxytocin bolus given with the anterior shoulder
Placenta accreta spectrum; routine misoprostol in the third stage
Endometritis; early clamping of the umbilical cord
questions.exp: Postpartum D&C carries the highest risk of Asherman syndrome; the best method of preventing PPH is active management of the third stage of labour. (Book p528)

questions.sec: PPH definitions, types & the 4 Ts
questions.q: Fill up: Primary postpartum haemorrhage is blood loss of ______ mL or more within 24 hours of birth, and the four Ts are tone, trauma, tissue and ______.
opts: 500; thrombin
1000; thrombus
500; traction
1000; tone
questions.exp: The four Ts are uterine tone, genital tract trauma, retained tissue and thrombin (coagulopathy); 500 mL defines PPH and 1000 mL severe PPH. (Book p528)

questions.sec: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
questions.q: Maternal risk factors for PPH include all EXCEPT:
opts: Primigravida
Previous history of PPH / advanced maternal age
Obesity / multigravida (↑ parity)
H/O PIH in current pregnancy / anemia
questions.exp: Maternal: previous PPH, advanced age, obesity, multigravida, PIH in current pregnancy, anemia. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
questions.q: Placental risk factors for PPH are:
opts: Placenta previa, abruptio placentae, placenta accreta spectrum and chorioamnionitis
A succenturiate lobe alone, which does not disturb the third stage
A velamentous cord insertion alone, which affects only the fetus
A circumvallate placenta alone, which is a harmless anatomical variant
questions.exp: Placental causes of PPH are previa, abruption, morbid adherence and infection; the others are variants that do not themselves provoke bleeding. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
questions.q: Uterine risk factors relate to overdistension, e.g.:
opts: Twin pregnancy, gestational diabetes, polyhydramnios, macrosomia and a fibroid uterus
A bicornuate uterus, which overdistends and weakens the myometrium
Cervical incompetence with a short painless cervix in the second trimester
A uterine septum, which stretches the lower segment during pregnancy
questions.exp: Overdistension of the uterus exhausts the myometrium; congenital anomalies do not overdistend it, though they can predispose otherwise. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
questions.q: Which statement about intrapartum risk factors for PPH is TRUE?
opts: Prolonged or precipitate labour, induction, instrumental delivery and general anaesthesia all raise the risk
Epidural analgesia and active management of the third stage raise the risk
Ambulation, continuous support and the left lateral position raise the risk
Oral fluids in labour and intermittent auscultation are intrapartum risk factors
questions.exp: Intrapartum risk factors exhaust or damage the uterus and birth canal; the measures in the other options are neutral or protective. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
questions.q: All of the following are specific risk factors for TRAUMATIC PPH EXCEPT:
opts: Anaemia in the mother before delivery
Instrumental delivery
Breech extraction
Obstructed labour with tachysystole
questions.exp: Traumatic PPH follows tears and lacerations from operative delivery, malpresentation, obstructed or very fast labour and high parity; anaemia is a maternal rather than a traumatic risk factor. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Risk factors for atonic & traumatic PPH
questions.q: All of the following predispose to uterine atony EXCEPT:
opts: A short uncomplicated first stage in a multiparous woman
Overdistension of the uterus from twins or polyhydramnios
Prolonged or augmented labour with an exhausted myometrium
Grand multiparity with a fibroid uterus
questions.exp: Atony follows overdistension, exhaustion, parity, fibroids, infection and anaesthesia; a quick uncomplicated labour does not exhaust the uterus. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
questions.q: First step in managing PPH (an obstetric emergency requiring a synchronised approach) is resuscitation, which includes all EXCEPT:
opts: Immediate hysterectomy
Large-bore IV cannula; blood samples for ABO/Rh, CBC, BT, CT; arrange blood
Crystalloids 1000 mL/min (RL/NS); ABC monitoring
Insert Foley's catheter
questions.exp: Resuscitation: IV cannula, blood samples, arrange blood, crystalloids 1000 mL/min, ABC, Foley catheter. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
questions.q: After resuscitation, per-abdominal uterine massage finds a well-contracted uterus with normal tone. This:
opts: Rules out atonic PPH and indicates traumatic PPH → P/V examination to find the cause
Confirms atonic PPH → uterotonics
Indicates retained placenta → MRP
Indicates uterine inversion → Johnson's method
questions.exp: Normal tone → atonic PPH ruled out → traumatic PPH → P/V examination. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
questions.q: If uterine tone is ↓ and maintained only by massage, this indicates ______; the next step is ______.
opts: Atonic PPH: look for retained products preventing contraction, then continue management of atony
Traumatic PPH: suture the cervical and vaginal lacerations under anaesthesia
Uterine inversion: replace the fundus back through the cervix under anaesthesia
Amniotic fluid embolism: transfer to intensive care for ventilatory support
questions.exp: A uterus that contracts only while being massaged is atonic; the next step is to exclude retained tissue that is sustaining the atony. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
questions.q: Immediately after delivery a woman loses 700 mL of blood. The uterus is boggy and reaches above the umbilicus, and the placenta has been expelled complete. What is the first step?
opts: Call for help, rub up a contraction and give oxytocin while resuscitating with fluids and oxygen
Examine the genital tract under anaesthesia before doing anything else
Insert uterine balloon tamponade immediately
Perform a manual exploration of the uterus straight away
questions.exp: A boggy uterus means atony, which is treated first by compression and uterotonics with simultaneous resuscitation; trauma is explored if bleeding persists. (Book p529)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: The three simultaneous steps in management of atonic PPH are:
opts: Bimanual uterine massage + injection tranexamic acid + uterotonic drug
Balloon tamponade + B-Lynch + hysterectomy
Oxytocin + misoprostol + carboprost
Foley + blood transfusion + massage
questions.exp: Bimanual massage (one hand on abdomen, one in vagina) + TXA + uterotonic. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: Tranexamic acid in PPH – timing and dose:
opts: Within 3 hours; 1 g in 100 mL of normal saline given intravenously over 20 minutes
Within 24 hours; 500 mg given by intramuscular injection
Within 1 hour; 2 g given as a rapid intravenous bolus
At any time after the bleed; 1 g given orally as a single dose
questions.exp: Tranexamic acid 1 g in 100 mL saline over 20 minutes must be given within three hours; faster administration causes hypotension. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: Tranexamic acid dose is repeated if bleeding:
opts: Persists ≥30 min or reappears within 24 h
Persists ≥5 min
Reappears after 1 week
Never repeated
questions.exp: Repeat if bleeding persists ≥30 min or reappears within 24 h. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: Oxytocin in atonic PPH – WHO status, dose and cautions:
opts: First-line drug recommended by WHO; 20-40 IU by infusion; avoid a bolus and avoid dextrose
Second-line drug; 10 IU by intravenous bolus, diluted in dextrose
Third-line drug; 5 IU intramuscularly, diluted in whatever fluid is to hand
Not used in postpartum haemorrhage because of the risk of water intoxication
questions.exp: Oxytocin is the WHO first-line uterotonic, given as 20-40 IU by infusion; boluses cause hypotension and dextrose causes hyponatraemia. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: Natural vs synthetic oxytocin:
opts: Natural – nonapeptide from paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus, stored in posterior pituitary, pulsatile release; synthetic – octapeptide stored at 2–8 °C
Natural – octapeptide from anterior pituitary; synthetic – nonapeptide at room temp
Natural – from supraoptic nucleus, stored in adrenal; synthetic – decapeptide
Both nonapeptides at room temperature
questions.exp: Natural: nonapeptide, paraventricular nucleus, posterior pituitary, pulsatile. Synthetic: octapeptide, 2–8 °C. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: Mechanism, half-life and kinetics of IM oxytocin:
opts: Raises intracellular calcium and decidual PGF2α; t½ 3-5 min; onset 3 min
Lowers intracellular calcium; t½ 40 min; onset 10 min
Raises cyclic AMP in the myometrium; t½ 1 h; onset 1 min
Blocks progesterone receptors; t½ 20 min; onset 5 min
questions.exp: IM oxytocin raises intracellular calcium and decidual PGF2α; half-life 3-5 minutes, onset 3 minutes, duration 1 hour, and it causes after-pains and milk ejection. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
questions.q: Fill up: Tranexamic acid is given as ______ g intravenously, and benefit is greatest when it is started within ______ hours of birth.
questions.exp: The WOMAN trial showed that 1 g of tranexamic acid given early, within three hours, reduces death from bleeding. (Book p530)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Methylergometrine – effect and dose:
opts: Tetanic contractions, so it cannot be used before delivery; 0.2 mg intramuscularly, repeated in 2-4 hours
Physiological contractions; 0.5 mg intravenously, stored in clear glass vials
Tetanic contractions; 1 mg orally six-hourly, and requiring refrigeration
Uterine relaxation; 0.2 mg subcutaneously as a single dose
questions.exp: Methylergometrine 0.2 mg intramuscularly gives a sustained tetanic contraction; it is avoided before delivery and given slowly, if at all, intravenously. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Contraindications to methylergometrine include all EXCEPT:
opts: Asthma
After delivery of first twin / heart disease / peripheral vascular disease
Uncomplicated pre-eclampsia / HELLP syndrome
Rh-negative pregnancy / HIV on protease inhibitors (relative)
questions.exp: Asthma is a C/I to carboprost, not ME. ME C/I: after 1st twin, heart disease, PVD, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, Rh-negative, HIV on PIs. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Syntometrine composition and note on carbetocin:
opts: 5 U oxytocin + 0.5 mg methylergometrine; expensive; carbetocin is used in AMTSL but not for PPH management
10 U oxytocin + 0.2 mg ME; cheap; carbetocin is PPH gold standard
5 U oxytocin + 250 mcg carboprost
0.5 mg ME + 600 mcg misoprostol
questions.exp: Syntometrine = 5 U oxytocin + 0.5 mg ME (expensive, not readily available); carbetocin not for PPH treatment. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Misoprostol in PPH – form, WHO strategy and dose:
opts: Prostaglandin E1, the only uterotonic available as a tablet; WHO recommends 800 microgram sublingually
Prostaglandin E2, given as an intracervical gel in a dose of 0.5 mg for cervical ripening
Prostaglandin F2 alpha, given as 250 microgram intramuscularly every fifteen minutes
An oxytocin analogue, given as a 100 microgram slow intravenous bolus after delivery
questions.exp: Misoprostol is PGE1 in tablet form; 800 microgram sublingually is the WHO regimen for prevention where oxytocin is unavailable. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Side effects and contraindication of misoprostol:
opts: Hyperthermia and shivering with nausea and vomiting; contraindicated with a scarred uterus
Hypertension and headache; contraindicated in established maternal heart disease
Bronchospasm, since misoprostol provokes an attack in asthmatic women
Profuse watery diarrhoea; contraindicated in maternal pulmonary hypertension
questions.exp: Misoprostol causes fever, shivering and gastrointestinal upset; unlike carboprost it is safe in asthma but risky with a uterine scar. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Carboprost (Hemabate) – class, status and dose:
opts: PGF2α; gold standard for PPH; 250 mcg IM every 15-40 min, max 8 doses; diarrhoea
PGE2; first-line alternative; 500 mcg by slow IV injection; pyrexia
PGE1; second-line agent; 1 mg IM repeated four-hourly; hypertension
PGI2; adjunct only; 100 mcg subcutaneously six-hourly; flushing
questions.exp: Carboprost (Hemabate) is PGF2α, the gold standard for PPH management, given as 250 mcg IM every 15-40 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses (2 mg); diarrhoea is the classic side effect. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
questions.q: Contraindications to carboprost and the status of dinoprostone:
opts: Asthma, pulmonary hypertension and suspected amniotic fluid embolism; dinoprostone is used off-label
Heart disease and Rh-negative status, with dinoprostone as the first-line drug
A scarred uterus only, with dinoprostone as the accepted gold standard
Diabetes mellitus, with dinoprostone given by intravenous infusion
questions.exp: Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma and pulmonary hypertension; dinoprostone (PGE2) is used off-label per vaginam or rectum. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Second-line uterotonics
questions.q: Match the second-line uterotonic with its dose and caveat — 1) Methylergometrine 2) Misoprostol 3) Carboprost … A) 800-1000 microgram rectally or sublingually, useful where injection or refrigeration is impractical B) 250 microgram intramuscularly every 15 minutes, contraindicated in asthma C) 0.2 mg intramuscularly, contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
questions.exp: Ergometrine raises blood pressure, misoprostol is the heat-stable standby, and carboprost is dangerous in asthma. (Book p531)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: Sequence of uterotonics in the PPH management protocol:
opts: Massage with tranexamic acid and oxytocin, then methylergometrine, then carboprost, with misoprostol as an add-on
Carboprost first, then oxytocin, then methylergometrine in that order
Misoprostol first, then oxytocin, then carboprost in that order
Methylergometrine first, then misoprostol, then oxytocin in that order
questions.exp: Oxytocin with tranexamic acid and massage is first line; ergometrine and then carboprost follow, with misoprostol as an adjunct. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: If unresponsive to drugs for >30 min, mechanical compression is used (continuing uterotonics) – principle and catheters:
opts: Warm saline in an intrauterine catheter compresses the venous sinuses; the Bakri balloon holds up to 500 mL
Cold saline packing through a Foley catheter is the only mechanical option available
An air-filled balloon inflated to 2000 mL in a Bakri catheter tamponades the uterus
Gauze packing of the uterine cavity is the current standard first-line technique
questions.exp: Intrauterine balloons tamponade by compressing the venous sinuses; the Bakri is filled with warm saline up to about 500 mL. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: If tamponade is responsive, the catheter is removed after ______; if bleeding continues with unstable vitals the next step is ______.
opts: 12–24 h; uterine artery ligation
1 h; hysterectomy
48 h; B-Lynch
6 h; embolization
questions.exp: Remove after 12–24 h if responsive; unstable vitals → uterine artery ligation. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: If bleeding continues but vitals are stable, the patient is shifted to OT with temporary measures such as:
opts: External aortic compression at the umbilicus, and a military anti-shock garment
The Trendelenburg position with cold packs applied to the abdomen
Vaginal packing with intravenous fluids and nothing further
Fundal pressure combined with an intravenous oxytocin bolus
questions.exp: Aortic compression and a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment buy time while the woman is transferred to theatre. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: Compression sutures for PPH include (m/c first):
opts: B-Lynch or Brace, then Hayman, Cho square, Pereira, Gunshella
McDonald, then Shirodkar, then the Wurm modification
O'Leary, then the Burch procedure, then Kelly plication
Halsted stitch, then the Lembert stitch, then the Connell stitch
questions.exp: Compression sutures for PPH are B-Lynch or Brace (commonest first), then Hayman, the Cho square sutures, Pereira and Gunshella. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: If bleeding continues after compression sutures – with radiointervention available : without radiointervention.
opts: With radiology: uterine artery embolisation if she is stable — without: stepwise devascularisation through to hysterectomy
With radiology: immediate hysterectomy — without: embolisation performed by the obstetric team
With radiology: internal iliac artery ligation — without: embolisation by interventional radiology
With radiology: uterine packing — without: immediate hysterectomy for every woman
questions.exp: Embolisation suits the stable woman where interventional radiology exists; otherwise stepwise devascularisation ends in hysterectomy. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
questions.q: Final steps if bleeding still continues – stable : unstable; and if hysterectomy fails to stop bleeding:
opts: Stable: ligation of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery — unstable: subtotal hysterectomy; then pelvic pressure packing
Stable: total hysterectomy — unstable: internal iliac ligation; then a gauze pack
Stable: embolisation — unstable: a B-Lynch suture; then a Bakri balloon
Stable: aortic ligation — unstable: oophorectomy; then a vaginal pack
questions.exp: If she is stable, vessel ligation can preserve the uterus; if she is not, subtotal hysterectomy is faster and safer, with packing as a bridge. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Management protocol: drugs, balloon, then surgery
questions.q: Bleeding continues in an atonic postpartum haemorrhage despite oxytocin, ergometrine and carboprost. The uterus is now contracted, the placenta was complete and the genital tract is intact. What is the next step?
opts: Insert a uterine balloon tamponade and prepare for surgical haemostasis if bleeding continues
Proceed directly to hysterectomy without any further measure
Give repeated doses of oxytocin and wait two hours
Repeat a manual removal of the placenta to be certain nothing remains
questions.exp: The escalation is balloon tamponade, then uterine compression sutures, vessel ligation and finally hysterectomy. (Book p532)

questions.sec: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
questions.q: Uterine artery ligation (O'Leary technique) is performed at:
opts: Where the artery turns upwards in the broad ligament, taking a bite of myometrium and staying close to the uterus
At its origin from the internal iliac artery, before the vessel crosses the lateral pelvic wall
At the level of the cervicovaginal junction, below the point where the vessels enter the cervix
At the cornual end of the uterus, where it anastomoses with the ovarian artery near the fundus
questions.exp: The O'Leary stitch is placed where the uterine artery turns up beside the uterus, including myometrium so the suture cannot slip and avoiding the ureter. (Book p533)

questions.sec: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
questions.q: Success rate of bilateral uterine artery ligation:
opts: About 85 per cent of cases, which is why it is attempted before hysterectomy
About 50 per cent of cases, so it is rarely worth attempting at all
About 99 per cent of cases, which makes hysterectomy almost unnecessary
About 30 per cent of cases, and only when performed before any drug
questions.exp: Bilateral uterine artery ligation controls bleeding in roughly 85 per cent of cases and preserves fertility, so it precedes hysterectomy. (Book p533)

questions.sec: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
questions.q: Shock index (SI) = heart rate ÷ systolic BP. Normal range and significance of SI ≥0.9:
opts: Normal is 0.5-0.7; a value of 0.9 or more indicates transfusion need and higher mortality
Normal is 0.9-1.2; a value of 1.5 or more is the threshold for transfusion
Normal is 0.3-0.5; a value of 0.7 or more means she needs intensive care
Normal is 1.0-1.5; a value of 2.0 or more means hysterectomy is required
questions.exp: The shock index is normally 0.5-0.7; 0.9 or above signals significant loss, the need for transfusion and raised mortality. (Book p533)

questions.sec: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
questions.q: Packing of the uterus for PPH is:
opts: An outdated method
The WHO first-line mechanical method
Preferred over balloon tamponade
Used only after hysterectomy
questions.exp: Uterine packing is outdated; balloon tamponade is used instead. (Book p533)

questions.sec: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
questions.q: Fill up: The shock index is calculated as ______ divided by ______, and a value above 0.9 suggests significant occult blood loss.
opts: pulse rate; systolic blood pressure
systolic blood pressure; pulse rate
diastolic pressure; pulse rate
blood loss; body weight
questions.exp: Heart rate and systolic pressure are the earliest vital signs to change in haemorrhage, so their ratio flags occult loss before hypotension appears. (Book p533)

questions.sec: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
questions.q: Features of the human placenta and the plane of separation:
opts: Deciduate, discoid, hemochorial; separates through zona spongiosa; most important factor = uterine contraction
Non-deciduate, zonary, epitheliochorial; zona basalis
Deciduate, cotyledonary, endotheliochorial; zona compacta
Non-deciduate, discoid, hemochorial; decidua parietalis
questions.exp: Deciduate, discoid, hemochorial; uterine contraction is most important; plane = zona spongiosa. (Book p534)

questions.sec: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
questions.q: Retained placenta (prolonged third stage) is defined as placenta not delivered:
opts: More than 30 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 15 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 60 minutes after the delivery of the baby
More than 10 minutes after the delivery of the baby
questions.exp: A third stage longer than 30 minutes is a prolonged third stage, and active intervention is considered once that time has passed. (Book p534)

questions.sec: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
questions.q: Placenta separated but not expelled (signs of separation present) = trapped placenta. Management:
opts: Empty the bladder, give oxytocin and repeat controlled cord traction; if it fails, manual removal under short anaesthesia
Empty the bladder, give oxytocin and repeat controlled cord traction; if it fails, proceed straight to hysterectomy
Leave it with antibiotics for 24 hours and reassess the next morning before intervening
Give misoprostol into the vagina and wait for spontaneous expulsion over the next six hours
questions.exp: A trapped placenta needs a full bladder emptied, a uterotonic and controlled cord traction, escalating to manual removal if it is still retained. (Book p534)

questions.sec: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
questions.q: Placenta attached to uterus but not invading myometrium – management:
opts: Oxytocin with controlled cord traction, then manual removal under anaesthesia if the placenta is still retained
Oxytocin with controlled cord traction, then immediate hysterectomy if the placenta is still retained
Methotrexate to dissolve the adherent placenta, followed by surgical evacuation a week later
Conservative management with antibiotics and observation for 24 hours before any intervention
questions.exp: When the placenta is simply adherent and not bleeding, oxytocin and controlled cord traction come first, with manual removal as the next step. (Book p534)

questions.sec: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
questions.q: Placenta invading the myometrium (morbidly adherent) is called ______ and managed by ______.
opts: Placenta accreta spectrum; hysterectomy
Trapped placenta; CCT
Placenta membranacea; curettage
Succenturiate placenta; MRP
questions.exp: Morbidly adherent = placenta accreta spectrum → hysterectomy. (Book p534)

questions.sec: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
questions.q: All of the following are recognised causes of retained placenta EXCEPT:
opts: A cervical tear sustained during instrumental delivery
Morbid adherence of the placenta to the myometrium
Uterine atony with failure of placental separation
A constriction ring trapping an already separated placenta
questions.exp: Retained placenta follows adherence, atony or entrapment; a cervical tear causes traumatic bleeding, not retention. (Book p534)

questions.sec: Placenta accreta spectrum
questions.q: Match PAS types by depth of chorionic villi – Accreta : Increta : Percreta.
opts: Accreta attached to myometrium; increta into myometrium; percreta to or through serosa
Accreta invades the myometrium; increta reaches the serosa; percreta is superficial
Accreta reaches the serosa; increta is superficial; percreta invades myometrium
Accreta into endometrium; increta to serosa; percreta into the bladder
questions.exp: By depth of chorionic villi: accreta is superficially attached to the myometrium (commonest), increta invades into the myometrium, and percreta is attached to or through the serosa. (Book p535)

questions.sec: Placenta accreta spectrum
questions.q: Risk factors and etiology of PAS:
opts: Placenta previa, a previous caesarean, curettage or myomectomy; the cause is defective decidua with absent Nitabuch's layer
Multiparity alone, through an excessively thick and vascular decidua basalis
A twin pregnancy alone, through an unusually thick Nitabuch layer
Maternal anaemia alone, through a hyperplastic and overactive endometrium
questions.exp: Accreta spectrum follows endometrial damage: previa, scar, curettage or myomectomy, with loss of the Nitabuch layer and decidua basalis. (Book p535)

questions.sec: Placenta accreta spectrum
questions.q: Investigation of choice for PAS and its findings:
opts: Ultrasound with Doppler: placental lakes, loss of the retroplacental clear zone and an interrupted bladder line
Magnetic resonance imaging: a snowstorm appearance filling the whole uterine cavity
Computed tomography: ring enhancement of the myometrium around the placental bed
Hysteroscopy: direct visualisation of chorionic villi inside the uterine cavity
questions.exp: Ultrasound with Doppler is the investigation of choice; the snowstorm appearance belongs to a molar pregnancy, not to accreta. (Book p535)

questions.sec: Placenta accreta spectrum
questions.q: Which of the following statements about placenta accreta is TRUE?
opts: Deficient decidua basalis prevents normal separation, so attempting manual removal causes torrential haemorrhage
Placenta accreta is commonest in a first pregnancy with no uterine surgery
Manual removal of the placenta is always safe and should be the first treatment
A normal third stage in a previous pregnancy rules out accreta in this one
questions.exp: Accreta follows endometrial damage from surgery or curettage, and the correct management leaves the placenta in situ rather than forcing separation. (Book p535)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
questions.q: Uterine inversion is ______; on inspection the os is ______ in inversion and ______ in uterine prolapse.
opts: Prolapse of the fundus into the uterine cavity; not visible; visible
Descent of cervix through introitus; visible; not visible
Rupture of the fundus; visible; visible
Retroversion of uterus; not visible; not visible
questions.exp: Inversion = fundus prolapses into cavity; os not visible in inversion but visible in prolapse. (Book p535)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
questions.q: Classification by time after delivery – Acute : Sub-acute : Chronic.
opts: <24 h : 24 h to 4 wks : ≥4 wks
<48 h : 2–7 days : >1 wk
questions.exp: Acute <24 h; sub-acute 24 h–4 wks; chronic ≥4 wks. (Book p536)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
questions.q: Classification by extent – 1st : 2nd : 3rd : 4th degree.
opts: Fundus into the cavity not beyond the os : fundus at the os : fundus outside the introitus : complete inversion
Dimple in the fundus : fundus at the os : fundus in the vagina : fundus outside
Fundus at the os : fundus in the vagina : fundus at the introitus : vagina everted
Fundus in the vagina : at the introitus : outside : with the bladder drawn in
questions.exp: By extent, inversion is graded: 1st the fundus dips into the cavity but not beyond the os; 2nd it reaches the os without protruding; 3rd it protrudes out of the introitus; 4th there is complete inversion of uterus and vagina. (Book p536)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
questions.q: The m/c cause of uterine inversion and the nature of shock:
opts: Iatrogenic from a mismanaged third stage; neurogenic shock first, then haemorrhagic shock
Spontaneous inversion with haemorrhagic shock alone and no neurogenic component at all
Associated with placenta previa, producing septic shock with rigors and hypotension
Caused by uterine fibroids, with cardiogenic shock from acute left ventricular failure
questions.exp: The commonest cause is mismanaged third stage; the initial neurogenic shock from stretching the pedicles is followed by haemorrhagic shock. (Book p536)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & features
questions.q: Match the degree of uterine inversion with its extent — 1) First degree 2) Second degree 3) Third degree … A) The fundus turns inwards but does not pass through the cervix B) The inverted fundus passes through the cervix and lies in the vagina C) The whole inverted uterus lies outside the vulva
questions.exp: Degrees are defined by how far the fundus has travelled: inside the cavity, through the cervix, or outside the vulva. (Book p536)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
questions.q: Examination findings in uterine inversion – P/A : P/V; and the clinical clue:
opts: A cup-like depression below the umbilicus, with a globular mass in the vagina and immediate shock
A hard contracted fundus, with the cervix easily visible and only slow bleeding
The fundus high above the umbilicus, with an empty vagina and fever
A Bandl's ring across the abdomen, with bulging membranes and late shock
questions.exp: The fundus is absent abdominally or dimpled, a globular mass fills the vagina, and shock is immediate and out of proportion. (Book p537)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: management
questions.q: First steps in managing acute uterine inversion:
opts: Call for help and resuscitate, stop uterotonics, then manual replacement
Give an oxytocin bolus, remove the placenta, then replace the uterus
Proceed to immediate hysterectomy through an abdominal incision
Pack the vagina firmly and wait for the uterus to contract
questions.exp: The first steps in acute uterine inversion are to call for help and resuscitate, stop uterotonics such as oxytocin, then replace the uterus manually (Johnson's method). (Book p537)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: management
questions.q: Principles of Johnson's method:
opts: Reposition last what prolapsed first; do not separate the placenta
Remove the placenta first, then replace the fundus into the pelvis
Push the cervix upwards first, then replace the uterine fundus
Apply steady traction to the cord until the uterus is fully delivered
questions.exp: Johnson's method: the part that prolapsed first is repositioned last, and the placenta is not separated, since separation increases haemorrhage. (Book p537)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: management
questions.q: If Johnson's method fails, the sequence is:
opts: Repeat replacement under anaesthesia with a uterine relaxant, then Huntington's or Haultain's abdominal route
Immediate hysterectomy, since further attempts at replacement are futile
Hydrostatic reduction by O'Sullivan's method followed by Spinelli's vaginal repair
Vaginal packing with an oxytocin infusion to contract the uterus down
questions.exp: If Johnson's vaginal replacement fails, the next attempt needs anaesthesia and a relaxant, with abdominal routes as the fallback. (Book p537)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: management
questions.q: Match – Huntington's : Haultain's : outdated methods.
opts: Huntington's: abdominal traction on the round ligaments — Haultain's: incising the constriction ring — outdated: O'Sullivan and Spinelli
Huntington's: vaginal repair — Haultain's: hydrostatic reduction — outdated: abdominal traction
Huntington's: incising the constriction ring — Haultain's: traction — outdated: embolisation
Huntington's: hydrostatic reduction — Haultain's: the Spinelli repair — outdated: abdominal traction
questions.exp: Huntington's pulls the fundus up with traction on the round ligaments; Haultain's incises the constriction ring from behind; the hydrostatic and Spinelli methods are historical. (Book p537)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: management
questions.q: Immediately after delivery of the placenta the uterus inverts through the cervix and the woman collapses with a pulse of 130/min and a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg. What is the correct sequence of management?
opts: Resuscitate, replace the uterus at once by hydrostatic or manual reduction, then give a uterotonic once it is back
Give oxytocin first so that the uterus contracts, and only then attempt replacement
Remove the placenta if it is still attached before attempting any replacement
Proceed straight to hysterectomy without attempting replacement
questions.exp: Replacement must not wait for the placenta or for uterotonics; shock is neurogenic as well as haemorrhagic and needs simultaneous resuscitation. (Book p537)

questions.sec: Uterine inversion: management
questions.q: Post-replacement management (in order):
opts: Stop uterine relaxant → remove placenta → start oxytocin → start antibiotics
Start oxytocin → remove placenta → stop relaxant → antibiotics
Remove placenta → start relaxant → oxytocin
Antibiotics → oxytocin → relaxant → placenta
questions.exp: 1 stop relaxant, 2 remove placenta, 3 start oxytocin, 4 antibiotics. (Book p538)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) – alias and incidence:
opts: Anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy, about 1 in 100,000 deliveries
Sheehan syndrome, occurring in about 1 in 1,000 deliveries
HELLP syndrome, occurring in about 1 in 10,000 deliveries
Mendelson syndrome, occurring in about 1 in 500 deliveries
questions.exp: Amniotic fluid embolism is also called anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy; it is rare at about 1 in 100,000 but catastrophic. (Book p538)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Pathophysiology of AFE begins with ______ and the amniotic fluid (fetal skin cells, debris, antigens) produces three effects:
opts: A breach of the maternal-fetal interface lets fluid into the circulation, causing pulmonary vasospasm and then coagulopathy
A hypotonic uterus fails to compress the placental bed, causing haemorrhage, sepsis and renal failure
Placental abruption releases thromboplastin into the circulation, producing coagulopathy alone
Cord prolapse compresses the umbilical vessels, producing fetal hypoxia with no maternal effects
questions.exp: Erratic contractions breach the interface and open venous sinuses; the fluid then causes pulmonary vasospasm, cardiac failure and consumptive coagulopathy. (Book p538)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Clinical phases of amniotic fluid embolism — Phase I : Phase II.
opts: Phase I: sudden hypoxia, hypotension and shock with little bleeding — Phase II: haemorrhage from disseminated intravascular coagulation
Phase I: heavy bleeding with an atonic uterus — Phase II: hypoxia from pulmonary vasospasm and right heart strain
Phase I: high fever with uterine tenderness — Phase II: septic shock with acute kidney injury
Phase I: severe hypertension and convulsions — Phase II: hepatic failure with profound hypoglycaemia
questions.exp: Phase I is respiratory and cardiovascular collapse with little bleeding, and phase II is the haemorrhagic phase from consumptive coagulopathy. (Book p538)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Clinical criteria for AFE diagnosis include all EXCEPT:
opts: High-grade fever
Unexplained shock with minimal bleeding / onset within 30 min of labour
Absent cardiopulmonary arrest (breathlessness & shock)
Overt DIC
questions.exp: Criteria: unexplained shock, onset within 30 min, breathlessness/shock, overt DIC, NO fever; also pulmonary vessel catheterisation. Management is ICU care; ↑ mortality. (Book p539)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Postpartum collapse – time of appearance: PPH : uterine inversion : AFE.
opts: Within 24 h : within 24 h : within 30 min of delivery
Within 30 min : within 24 h : within 1 wk
Within 1 h : within 30 min : within 24 h
All within 30 min
questions.exp: PPH and inversion within 24 h; AFE within 30 min. (Book p539)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Postpartum collapse examination – P/A and P/V findings: PPH : uterine inversion : AFE.
opts: PPH: poor tone and heavy loss — inversion: a cup-like depression and a vaginal mass — AFE: both examination findings normal
PPH: entirely normal findings — inversion: poor uterine tone — AFE: a cup-like depression
PPH: a globular vaginal mass — inversion: heavy bleeding — AFE: poor uterine tone
All three conditions give entirely normal findings on both examinations
questions.exp: Postpartum collapse is triaged by examination: bleeding with an atonic uterus, an inverted uterus felt in the vagina, or a normal examination with sudden collapse from embolism. (Book p539)

questions.sec: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
questions.q: Fill up: Amniotic fluid embolism typically begins with sudden ______ and ______, and is followed rapidly by bleeding from disseminated intravascular coagulation.
opts: dyspnoea with cyanosis; hypotension and shock
fever with rigor; severe hypertension
abdominal pain; progressive jaundice
headache; loss of vision
questions.exp: The classic presentation is abrupt respiratory collapse and cardiovascular collapse during labour or soon after delivery, then coagulopathy. (Book p539)

units.title: PPH: definitions, types & the 4 Ts

units.title: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH
units.guide: Run the six-point resuscitation, then use per-abdominal massage to split atonic from traumatic PPH and decide the next examination. Focus for this checkpoint: Initial management: resuscitation & atonic vs traumatic PPH.

units.title: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid
units.guide: Perform bimanual massage, give tranexamic acid at the right dose and timing, and start the WHO first-choice uterotonic. Focus for this checkpoint: Atonic PPH: three simultaneous steps & tranexamic acid.

units.title: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost
units.guide: Dose each second-line drug, identify its unique contraindications and side effects, and know which is the gold standard. Focus for this checkpoint: Second-line uterotonics: methylergometrine, syntometrine, misoprostol & carboprost.

units.title: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery
units.guide: Follow the escalation ladder from first-line uterotonics through balloon tamponade, compression sutures, devascularisation and hysterectomy. Focus for this checkpoint: Management protocol: drugs → balloon tamponade → surgery.

units.title: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing
units.guide: Place the O'Leary suture correctly, quote its success rate, compute the shock index and remember which old method is obsolete. Focus for this checkpoint: Uterine artery ligation, shock index & packing.

units.title: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm
units.guide: Define retained placenta and manage each of its three causes – trapped, adherent-non-invasive and morbidly adherent. Focus for this checkpoint: Retained placenta: causes & management algorithm.

units.title: Placenta accreta spectrum
units.guide: Grade accreta, increta and percreta by depth, know the risk factors, etiology, Doppler signs and definitive treatment. Focus for this checkpoint: Placenta accreta spectrum.

units.title: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features
units.guide: Distinguish inversion from prolapse, classify by time and degree, and recognise the neurogenic-then-hemorrhagic shock picture. Focus for this checkpoint: Uterine inversion: definition, classification & clinical features.

units.title: Uterine inversion: management
units.guide: Apply Johnson's manual replacement principles, know the surgical fall-backs and outdated methods, and the four post-replacement steps. Focus for this checkpoint: Uterine inversion: management.

units.title: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse
units.guide: Explain AFE pathophysiology and its two clinical phases, the clinical diagnostic criteria, and differentiate the three causes of postpartum collapse. Focus for this checkpoint: Amniotic fluid embolism & postpartum collapse.
